name: Google Patents by inventor (through SerpApi)
holds: every patent under an inventor's name, from every patent office, the US ones back to 1790 and Japan's from 1885: the one way to find a patent from before 1976 by who made it. The query is the inventor's name and nothing else, in Latin letters as a patent office wrote it (Jokichi Takamine), and again family name first
key_from: https://serpapi.com (250 searches a month free; each search here is one of them)
title: {/title}

name: Google Patents by words (through SerpApi)
holds: patents of every patent office by the words in them: an invention, a firm, a place. For a person use serpapi-inventor
key_from: https://serpapi.com (250 searches a month free; each search here is one of them)
title: {/title}

name: European Patent Office, by inventor (Espacenet)
holds: the patents of most of the world's patent offices (Japan, the United States, Britain, Germany, France and many more, a good part of them from before 1920), found by the inventor's name. The query is the name and nothing else. For a Japanese, Chinese or Korean inventor search the name in its own script FIRST (山田太郎): patents of the last decades carry it, and it sets the person apart from everybody whose name only sounds the same. A name is matched as it is written, so search an old character form and the modern one separately (髙橋 and 高橋, 眞 and 真). Then search it in Latin letters as a patent office wrote it (Taro Yamada, or Yamada Taro), which is the only form older patents and other countries have. Several people share a romanised name, and the newest patents come first: give the years the person could have been at work (from_year, to_year), and let the year, the country, the applicant and the subject say whether a patent is this person's. Where the answer gives the inventor's name in its own script, compare it with the person's: the same reading written with other characters is somebody else
key_from: https://developers.epo.org (free: register, add an app, and it shows a consumer key and a consumer secret; about 4 GB of answers a week)
title: {/exchange-document/bibliographic-data/invention-title}

name: European Patent Office, by applicant (Espacenet)
holds: the same patents, found by who applied for them: a company a person founded or worked for, or the person themselves. The query is the applicant's name and nothing else, in Latin letters
key_from: https://developers.epo.org (free: register, add an app, and it shows a consumer key and a consumer secret; about 4 GB of answers a week)
title: {/exchange-document/bibliographic-data/invention-title}

name: European Patent Office, by a query of several parts (Espacenet)
holds: the same patents, asked for with more than one condition at once, which is how one person is told from their namesakes. The query is written in the office's own short language, copied from these examples with your own words in them: in="Yamada Taro" and pa=hitachi   (an inventor at a firm) · in="Yamada Taro" and ti=turbine   (an inventor and a word of the title) · in="山田太郎" and pd>=1990 and pd<=2005   (an inventor in the years given) · pa="Yamada Seisakusho"   (a firm). in is the inventor, pa the applicant, ti a word of the title, pd the year of publication
key_from: https://developers.epo.org (free: register, add an app, and it shows a consumer key and a consumer secret; about 4 GB of answers a week)
title: {/exchange-document/bibliographic-data/invention-title}
